standards.title: ZLIB Compressed Data Format Specification version 3.3

normative_inventory.scope: Atomic case-insensitive normative must, should, and recommended clauses in pre-BCP 14 prose; may, optional, and need-not permissions are excluded.

requirements.summary: The bounded zlib decoder accepts and decompresses conforming byte-aligned zlib streams within the caller's explicit resource contract.
The Deflate content encoder produces a complete conforming zlib wrapper rather than a raw DEFLATE stream.
Encoded CMF and FLG bytes satisfy the RFC modulo-31 FCHECK invariant.
The compressor emits the required CMF and FLG header and the correct terminal ADLER32 checksum.
HTTP Deflate encoding rejects caller dictionary state and therefore never sets FDICT for this embedding format.
The decoder validates CMF, FLG, and ADLER32 independently and reports malformed input on any incorrect value.
A syntactically checkable header using an unsupported compression method is rejected as invalid encoding.
An FDICT stream whose DICTID has no authorized preset dictionary is rejected with a typed dictionary error.
A zlib embedding format must support every preset dictionary that the embedding format specifies.
requirements.reason: The HTTP Deflate content coding implemented here specifies no zlib preset dictionaries; dictionary transport uses separately typed Brotli and Zstandard codings and never reaches the zlib wrapper.

requirements.summary: Because HTTP Deflate defines no preset dictionary, every received zlib stream carrying FDICT is rejected.
A compressor and decompressor using the optional zlib dictionary feature must use exactly the same dictionary.
requirements.reason: The public HTTP Deflate coding rejects dictionaries on both encode and decode, so no zlib preset-dictionary session can be established or mismatched.

requirements.summary: A standard data format using zlib preset dictionaries must define its allowed dictionaries precisely.
requirements.reason: This package implements existing HTTP content codings and does not define a standard data format that embeds zlib with the optional preset-dictionary feature.

requirements.summary: The ADLER32 calculation begins with the required recommended initial checksum value of one.

standards.title: DEFLATE Compressed Data Format Specification version 1.3

normative_inventory.scope: Atomic case-insensitive normative must, should, and recommended clauses in pre-BCP 14 prose; may, optional, and need-not permissions are excluded.

requirements.summary: The bounded DEFLATE decoder accepts conforming stored, fixed-Huffman, dynamic-Huffman, and maximum-range streams.
The Deflate content encoder emits complete conforming DEFLATE data inside the required zlib wrapper.
DEFLATE block fields and Huffman codes use the RFC's defined bit-to-byte packing order without host-endian dependence.
The compressor does not emit Huffman codes beyond the format maxima and the decoder rejects malformed dynamic trees.
Symbols with zero bit length receive no Huffman value in emitted trees and malformed tree assignments are rejected.
Length and distance extra-bit integers are interpreted least-significant bit first as corrected by reported erratum 7764.
Zero-length literal, length, and distance symbols do not participate in Huffman tree construction.
The decoder accepts the maximum 258-byte match and 32768-byte backward distance defined by DEFLATE.
The streaming decoder accepts large and multi-block representations subject only to the caller's explicit finite resource limits.
A compressor implementor is strongly recommended to follow the historical algorithm described to avoid then-relevant patent coverage.
requirements.reason: The repository does not implement or redistribute a DEFLATE compression algorithm; it uses the explicitly permitted OTP runtime zlib service, and this historical patent rationale is not wire behavior.

requirements.summary: Systems using DEFLATE provide an integrity check for compressed data instead of silently accepting corruption.

entries.reason: The published MSB-first sentence conflicts with the section 3.1 packing rule and interoperable DEFLATE wire behavior; the proposed LSB-first correction is applied.
The proposed insertion of the word length disambiguates the prose but does not alter the defined Huffman construction or interoperable decoder behavior.

requirements.summary: The bounded gzip decoder accepts conforming minimal, optional-header, and concatenated-member representations.
The gzip encoder emits a deterministic complete member with a conforming header, DEFLATE payload, and trailer.
An emitted optional original filename must consist only of ISO 8859-1 characters.
requirements.reason: The public HTTP gzip encoder accepts content bytes only and always emits the minimal deterministic header with FNAME clear, so it cannot emit filename metadata in any character set.

requirements.summary: A filename from an operating system using another character set must be translated into ISO 8859-1.
requirements.reason: No filesystem filename or filename encoding enters the content-coding API and the encoder always leaves FNAME clear; operating-system name translation is therefore unreachable.

requirements.summary: An emitted optional gzip comment must consist only of ISO 8859-1 characters.
requirements.reason: The encoder exposes no comment metadata and emits the deterministic minimal gzip header with FCOMMENT clear, so it cannot serialize a nonconforming comment.

requirements.summary: Line breaks in an emitted optional gzip comment should use one line-feed byte.
requirements.reason: The public encoder never emits FCOMMENT and accepts no comment text, leaving no line-ending metadata to normalize.

requirements.summary: The three reserved bits in every emitted gzip FLG byte are zero.
The compressor emits correct ID1, ID2, compression method, CRC32, and uncompressed input size fields.
The compliant gzip compressor sets every reserved header flag bit to zero.
The decoder validates both gzip identification bytes and compression method and rejects every incorrect value.
The decoder parses or skips bounded FEXTRA, XLEN, FNAME, FCOMMENT, and FHCRC fields before the compressed payload.
A gzip member with any nonzero reserved FLG bit is rejected rather than misparsed as a known header layout.
The gzip decoder validates the CRC32 integrity field and fails closed on compressed-data corruption.

requirements.summary: Every handshake message carrying one of these extensions is covered by the handshake transcript hash, because the transcript is fed each message whole rather than selectively.
A client that cannot know whether its resumption request will be accepted still sends the extensions it would send for a full handshake.
A server resuming an older session ignores these extensions and answers without them.
requirements.reason: This is the TLS 1.2 abbreviated handshake, where resuming replays a previous session's parameters. TLS 1.3 has no such handshake: resumption is a pre-shared key offered in a full ClientHello, every extension is negotiated afresh, and this package speaks TLS 1.3 alone.

requirements.summary: The server_name extension_data is a ServerNameList, encoded and decoded as the structure the section defines rather than as a bare name.
A ServerNameList carries at most one name of a given name_type: exactly one host_name entry is encoded, and decoding refuses a list shaped any other way.
A server that understands the extension but not the name either aborts with unrecognized_name or continues with a certificate it does have.
A warning-level unrecognized_name alert is not sent, because what a client does on receiving one is not predictable.
A data structure for a future NameType begins with a sixteen-bit length so that an implementation which does not know the type can still skip it.
requirements.reason: This binds whoever defines a new NameType, and this package defines none. What it does on the reading side is what the rule exists to permit: a list whose single entry is not host_name is refused rather than guessed at, and the entry's own length prefix is what bounds the read.

requirements.summary: A client includes the server_name extension whenever it located the server by a domain name, which is every connection here that was not made to an address literal.
A server that acted on the name includes a server_name extension in its own hello.
The server's echoed server_name extension carries an empty extension_data rather than repeating the name.
A resumption request carries the same server_name the full handshake carried, which here is guaranteed because the ticket is bound to that name and refused against another.
A session is not resumed when the server_name offered differs from the one the session was established with: the ticket records the name and is refused against any other.
A server hello for a resumed session carries no server_name extension.
requirements.reason: The rule is about the TLS 1.2 abbreviated handshake's ServerHello. In TLS 1.3 a resumed connection is a full handshake with a pre-shared key, and this server's hello never carries a server_name extension on any path: the echo it does send belongs to EncryptedExtensions.

requirements.summary: Where an application protocol negotiated a server name before upgrading to TLS, the extension carries the same name.
A client does not ask for a different server name in the application protocol once one was established in the handshake.
The max_fragment_length extension_data carries the enumerated fragment length being requested.
requirements.reason: The max_fragment_length extension is not offered and not acted on. TLS 1.3 supersedes it with record_size_limit, and QUIC sizes its own records from the path rather than negotiating a fragment length. A peer that sends it anyway is decoded as a bounded opaque extension and nothing reads its value, so none of this section's processing is ever entered.

An earlier in-flight packet is declared lost after a later same-space packet is acknowledged and the time threshold passes.
The time loss threshold is always at least the local timer granularity.
A not-yet-lost packet before the largest ACK schedules its remaining time-threshold deadline.
Time-threshold loss detection uses the recommended nine-eighths RTT multiplier.
The live recovery owner uses the recommended one millisecond timer granularity.
PTO expiry increments backoff and requests probes without declaring any outstanding packet lost.
The four-times RTT variation component floors every PTO base at timer granularity.
The connection deadline selects the earlier Initial or Handshake recovery timer.
Application Data recovery cannot arm a PTO before handshake confirmation.
Sending, newly acknowledging, or discarding keys recomputes recovery from current packet state and RTT.
Every PTO expiration increments one bounded exponent shared across packet number spaces.
A present time-threshold loss deadline suppresses the packet space PTO deadline.
A path without historical RTT starts from the recommended 333 millisecond estimate.
A PATH_CHALLENGE round trip should not become a normal RTT estimator sample.
requirements.reason: The implementation does not exercise the optional preceding behavior of deriving a new-path initial RTT from PATH_CHALLENGE delay; path validation time never enters the RTT estimator.

requirements.summary: Discarding Initial or Handshake keys removes that space's loss and PTO timer state.

An amplification-blocked server arms no PTO it lacks budget to transmit, and a prepared probe which exhausts the remaining credit is retained as pending work rather than converted into a fatal connection error.
An unconfirmed client without a Handshake ACK arms an anti-deadlock PTO even with no packet in flight.
The anti-deadlock PTO selects a Handshake probe whenever Handshake write keys exist.
Without Handshake keys, anti-deadlock recovery selects Initial and the wire sender pads its datagram to 1200 bytes.

Every fired PTO makes at least one ack-eliciting probe ready in the expired packet space: already queued delivery work is preferred, otherwise ownership of the oldest reliable outstanding frame is transferred, and only an empty space falls back to PING.
The bounded PTO allowance can only be consumed by ack-eliciting in-flight packets; automatic probe work is either reliable delivery state transferred exactly once or a PING fallback.
A PTO should also coalesce an ack-eliciting probe from another packet space that has in-flight data.
Queued control, CRYPTO, or stream delivery work is used as the probe before recovery retransmission or a PING fallback, without dropping later data that can share the packet.
When no application or retransmission data exists, PTO sends a PING to rearm recovery.
Discarding packet-protection keys clears every sent-packet recovery record for that space.
The same key-discard transition removes all affected in-flight bytes from congestion accounting.
Selecting CUBIC preserves bounded flight, pacing, loss response, ECN response, and application-limited safeguards.
Normal in-flight sends are refused when their bytes would exceed cwnd; only an active PTO allowance bypasses the gate.
NewReno starts at min(10 times max_datagram_size, max(14720, twice max_datagram_size)).
A maximum datagram size change should recalculate an otherwise unchanged initial congestion window.
requirements.reason: A validated path-size change immediately updates the controller's datagram unit and minimum-window floor, but deliberately preserves the accumulated congestion window instead of guessing whether it still represents the initial flight.

requirements.summary: A handshake-only datagram-size reduction should reset cwnd to the new initial value.
requirements.reason: The path-size adapter has no trustworthy signal that a decrease occurred specifically to complete the handshake, so it preserves current cwnd while updating the datagram unit and reduction floor.

requirements.summary: NewReno loss and persistent-congestion reductions floor cwnd at two maximum datagrams.
A first packet loss or ECN-CE increase exits NewReno slow start into recovery.
Entering a NewReno recovery period sets ssthresh to half cwnd, bounded by the minimum window.
The congestion window is reduced immediately on recovery entry and remains reduced when recovery exits.
Congestion avoidance adds at most one maximum datagram after one whole congestion window is acknowledged.
Loss classification retains every packet sent after the earliest acknowledged packet in its number space.
A granted PTO probe bypasses a full congestion window without opening the gate for ordinary sends.
PTO probe bytes enter congestion and a bounded recovery ledger even when they exceed cwnd.
Persistent-congestion duration multiplies the current PTO base by the recommended threshold of three.
Both boundary packets used to establish a persistent-congestion interval are ack-eliciting.
Persistent congestion cannot start unless a real RTT sample existed when both boundary packets were sent.
Persistent-congestion interval construction should compare send times across all packet number spaces.
requirements.reason: The bounded recovery ledger intentionally uses the RFC-permitted fallback of the packet space that was acknowledged; it retains ACK barriers in that space but does not hold a second cross-space send-time index.

requirements.summary: A live persistent-congestion event collapses cwnd to the controller's minimum window.

Every in-flight live send reserves finite pacing credit derived from current cwnd and smoothed RTT. Pending work arms its exact release, including an immediate wake when it is already pacing-ready, while a full congestion window suppresses that zero-delay retry.
A bounded token-bucket pacer limits every in-flight burst and returns an exact release deadline.
The default pacer burst is bounded to ten current path-sized datagrams, matching the initial window.
Packets containing only ACK frames bypass pacing because they are not classified in flight.
Neither slow start nor congestion avoidance grows cwnd when the pre-ACK flight did not fill it.
An ACK batch snapshots full utilization before removing packets, so pacing delay alone cannot suppress legitimate growth.

entries.reason: The verified correction computes the rttvar sample against the old smoothed_rtt before updating smoothed_rtt; update_existing preserves that ordering.

requirements.summary: Every received element is parsed against an explicit grammar and an explicit bound, and a value that does not fit either is a typed error rather than something worked around.

A received element is interpreted by the rules of the field it belongs to: the framing fields, the control data, and the conditional fields each have their own validator rather than a shared string comparison.
Nothing is carried between two requests on one connection: each is dispatched with its own context, and the connection holds no identity a later request could inherit.
The request line bound is explicit and its configured value is at or above the octet count this clause names.
A request with an empty host is refused before it is built, so no such URI is generated.
A received authority that is empty is a typed error rather than a request with no target.
The same check binds both schemes, because it is the authority that is validated rather than the scheme that qualifies it.

An https request opens a TLS connection with peer verification before any byte of it is written; there is no path that sends one in the clear.
Two resources are not identified by URIs that normalize to the same thing.

A certificate that is not valid for the origin fails the connection with a typed error; there is no path that asks a user or continues anyway.
The failure is surfaced as a typed error naming its reason, which is the audit surface a library has: it writes no log of its own, and the caller that receives the error is the one with one.
The connection is closed at the failure rather than kept for a retry.

entries.reason: An editorial correction inside the appendix that collects changes from RFC 7231. It states nothing normative.

The rejected correction concerned how the trailer field section describes merging. This package returns a trailer block separately and refuses the field names that may not be trailed, which satisfies the published text and the proposed one alike.
The correction clarifies the permanent-redirect section's own wording. This client preserves the method and body for the redirect statuses that define no rewrite, which is the corrected reading.
The correction clarifies how a media-range weight is written. Proactive content negotiation is not implemented here, so neither text describes anything this package does.
The correction clarifies a byte-range example. Range requests are not implemented here.
The correction clarifies how a charset parameter is described. Which media type a representation carries is the caller's here; this package neither reads nor writes one.
The rejected correction concerned the unauthorized-response section. Authentication is the caller's here: this package parses no challenge and implements no scheme.
The rejected correction concerned the content-coding section's own wording. The compression module is handed a typed coding and returns bytes; it names none.

The rejected correction concerned how the Content-Length section describes a value that disagrees with the content. This parser refuses a message whose declared length is not a single decimal value and refuses a body that ends short of it, under either text.

The rejected correction concerned the redirection section's own wording. This client follows the statuses that define a redirect, preserves the method except where a rewrite is defined, and bounds how many it follows, under either text.
An editorial correction inside the appendix that collects changes from RFC 7232 through RFC 7235. It states nothing normative.
The rejected correction concerned how the status code section describes an unrecognized code. This client treats one by its class, which is what the published text asks for.

Trailer fields are retained separately from header fields and are rebuilt as trailers, so neither is ever served as the other.
A revalidating response updates the stored header fields, replacing those it supplies.

It stores a response only while that response is explicitly fresh and serves it only until that freshness lapses, at which point the entry is gone and the request goes to the origin as though nothing had been stored. One exchange owns its connection for its lifetime, so the list of outstanding requests has exactly one entry and the association cannot be lost.

The exchange watches for a response while it is still writing a request body, which is what lets an early error response end the write.
An error response while the body is going out ends the exchange and closes the connection rather than finishing the write into a socket nobody is reading.
Both sides announce it: the client adds the close option when it will not reuse the connection, and the server adds it to the last response it will send.
The exchange that announced the close is the last one on that connection: it is not returned to the pool.
It closes the connection once that response has been read, through the guard that claims the close exactly once.

That final response carries the close option itself.
Bytes already buffered after a request that ends the connection are discarded rather than dispatched, which a test pins with pipelined bytes behind a rejected CONNECT.

requirements.summary: The only protocol identifier this package offers or selects for HTTP/2 is the TLS one; nothing names the cleartext identifier.
A connection begins with the preface: the client writes the magic and its SETTINGS, and the server writes its SETTINGS, before either reads anything else.
Every HTTP/2 connection negotiates its protocol through ALPN; the transport advertises and selects it rather than assuming a version.
The server's half of the preface is its SETTINGS frame, written before it reads the client's.
The magic octets are followed immediately by a SETTINGS frame, which the initial-bytes builder emits as one sequence.
The first frame a peer sends has to be a SETTINGS frame without the acknowledgement flag, and anything else is a typed connection error.
Receiving the peer's SETTINGS applies its values and emits the acknowledgement as part of the same transition.
A preface that does not match is refused as soon as the bytes that differ arrive, without waiting for the rest.
What this endpoint writes is bounded by the peer's advertised maximum frame size rather than by its own.
A frame whose type this endpoint does not know is preserved by the decoder and ignored by the connection rather than refused.
Only the flags each frame type defines are read; the rest of the byte is carried and never consulted.
The encoder writes the flags a frame type defines and zero elsewhere, so an unused flag cannot be set on the way out.
The reserved bit of the stream identifier is written as zero.
It is masked off on receipt rather than read, so a peer that sets it changes nothing.
The decoder's payload bound is explicit and its configured floor is the size this clause requires every implementation to accept.
A frame longer than the advertised maximum is refused from its header, before its payload is read or retained.
A length error on a frame that would have changed connection state ends the connection rather than one stream, which is what the fixed-length checks produce.
A field block is assembled from its opening frame and the continuations that follow it on the same stream; any other frame in between is a typed error.
A field block that does not decode is a connection error carrying the compression code rather than a stream error.
Every decoder failure maps to that one code, so a malformed block cannot be mistaken for a malformed message.
A reduction is signalled in the next field block: the encoder holds the pending capacity change and emits the minimum it passed through and the final value before any field.
A table size update is admitted only at the start of a block and is bounded by the acknowledged maximum; one that arrives later is a typed decoder error.
An idle stream admits a header section and a priority signal; any other frame on one is a typed state error.
A client refuses a header section on an even-numbered stream it did not have reserved, which the registry decides from the identifier's parity.
A reserved stream admits a header section, a reset, and a priority signal on the way out, and the state machine refuses anything else.
A stream reserved by the peer admits a reset, a priority signal, and a window update, and nothing else.
The sending side of such a stream is the same three frames.
A stream the peer has half closed admits a header section, a reset, and a priority signal; data on it is a typed error.
A closed stream admits a window update, a priority signal, and a reset; anything else is a typed error rather than data accepted after the end.
Nothing but a priority signal is written on a closed stream, which the send side of the state machine refuses.
A field block on a closed stream is still decoded so the compression context stays consistent, and then discarded.
A closed stream is released by the transition that closed it rather than by a timer, which is what releases its admission slot.
Every frame this state machine does not expressly permit in a state is a typed error rather than something ignored.
A locally opened stream takes the next identifier of this endpoint's own parity.
The same rule gives a server even identifiers, from the same allocation.
A peer identifier at or below the highest already seen is refused, and a locally opened one always increases.
A parity or ordering violation is a typed connection error rather than a new stream.
Opening a local stream is admitted against the peer's advertised concurrency and refused when it would exceed it.
A peer header section past this endpoint's own advertised limit is a typed error rather than an extra stream.
Every data write is consumed from both the connection and the stream window, and a write with no credit is held rather than sent.
Frames are read and parsed as they arrive rather than after a message completes, and receive credit is released as the application consumes the body.
Responses are scheduled by the extensible priority scheme rather than by arrival alone, with the request's own signal used until a newer update replaces it.
A transition returns one typed error and stops, so a frame that breaks several rules is reported once.
The drain path sends one GOAWAY carrying one code, and a later one may only narrow the identifier.
A connection error is returned from the transition rather than swallowed, and the caller closes on it.
A connection error is announced with GOAWAY naming the last stream this endpoint processed before the connection is closed.
The connection is closed after that frame rather than kept for more frames.
A graceful stop announces itself the same way before it closes.
Frames that were already in flight for a stream this endpoint reset are processed for their connection-level effect and then discarded.
A reset closes the stream, and a second reset for one already closed changes nothing rather than emitting another frame.
Receiving a reset closes the stream without producing one in reply.
An unknown setting identifier, frame type, or error code is carried and read by nothing rather than refused.
A frame of an unknown type is discarded after the connection has its initial settings.
Any frame between a header section and its continuations is a typed error, whether its type is known or not.
An extension avoids changing the protocol elements this document defines.

The same holds for a header section: none is written padded.

Another frame, or a continuation for a different stream, is a typed connection error.

Its length is fixed and any other is a typed size error.

Frames already in flight for a stream this endpoint reset are still processed for their connection-level effect.

A concurrency of zero is applied like any other value: it admits no new stream and nothing else about it changes.
This server never advertises zero: a listener that does not want requests drains and closes instead.
An initial window size past the flow-control maximum is a typed range error.
A maximum frame size outside the stated range is refused the same way.
Both refusals are connection errors rather than settings that are clamped.
An identifier this endpoint does not know is decoded, carried, and applied to nothing.
The peer view is updated and the acknowledgement emitted in one transition, so the values are in force before the peer sees the acknowledgement.
Values are applied in the order they appear, so a repeated identifier ends at its last value and the window delta is reported from that.
An identifier with no meaning here changes nothing about the peer view.
The acknowledgement is one of the actions that transition returns rather than something queued behind other work.
A promised stream identifier is a valid next identifier for its sender.

requirements.summary: Promises are allocated in sequence from zero, which is what makes the allowed maximum a bound rather than a set.
A push stream whose push ID was never permitted is a typed not-allowed error, which the registry raises before the stream is opened.
Promising one push ID twice with different fields is a typed inconsistency rather than a second promise.
The comparison is of the field list as promised, so a reordering is a mismatch too.
A promised request is validated as a request, so its authority is one this endpoint could have answered rather than an arbitrary string.
A promise for an origin this connection was not opened for is refused rather than verified separately, because this client associates one origin with one connection.
That refusal is what keeps the server from becoming authoritative for an origin it was not validated for.
A promise the caller does not want is cancelled through the public cancellation path, which announces the cancellation to the server.
A cancelled push is terminal: its stream is released and its bytes are not delivered.
A push stream cannot be opened before its promise exists: opening one for an unpromised push ID is a typed error.
A push stream whose promise never arrives expires on a bounded timer rather than being held indefinitely, and its buffered data is dropped with it.
A promised request that is not safe, or that carries content, is refused outright, so nothing uncacheable reaches a cache through this path.
An idle connection ends on its own bounded timer and a later request opens a new one; nothing tries to reuse a connection past the idle period.
The server's keepalive is bounded and off by default, so an idle connection is allowed to end rather than held open.
Sending GOAWAY names a cutoff and everything past it is rejected rather than left waiting.
Requests arriving after the cutoff keep being rejected for as long as the drain lasts.
A peer's GOAWAY stops new requests and new promises on that connection, and the requests past its identifier are detached as retryable.
A graceful stop begins with GOAWAY rather than a close, which is what the two-stage drain is.
A second GOAWAY may only narrow: the drain refines its cutoff downward and never upward.
Receiving a larger identifier than before is a typed error that becomes the id-error connection code.
A completed graceful shutdown closes with the no-error code.
Only the requests a GOAWAY named as past its cutoff are reported retryable; a connection that ends without one leaves every request in flight reported as a failure the caller must decide about.
The transport parameters this server offers permit the unidirectional streams HTTP/3 needs before any of them is opened.
The configured request-stream concurrency is explicit and its default is at or above the hundred this clause names.
A bidirectional stream from the server is refused: the request-stream validator admits only client-initiated bidirectional identifiers.
The three critical streams are opened together at bootstrap, so the parameters that admit them are the ones this endpoint offers.
Each unidirectional stream is opened with credit from the configured limits rather than from a default the peer would have to guess.
Bootstrap is the first thing a connection does and opens all three before any request stream exists.
A stream whose type this endpoint does not know is not registered: its preface decodes to an unknown type and the stream is abandoned rather than read further.
Aborting such a stream uses the stream-creation error code.
An unknown stream type ends that stream and nothing else: the connection state is untouched by it.
The preface is read before anything is decided about the stream, and a truncated one is retained rather than discarded.
The stream types that change connection state are the ones this registry knows, and each is registered rather than discarded.
A unidirectional stream that ends before its preface is complete is a truncated preface rather than a connection failure.
Bootstrap opens exactly one control stream and writes SETTINGS as its first frame.
Any other frame first on a peer's control stream is the typed missing-settings error.
A second stream claiming to be a control stream is a typed duplicate rather than a replacement.
Nothing in this endpoint closes its own control stream; the drain closes the connection instead.
No path resets or stops a peer's critical stream either.
A critical stream closing or being reset is the closed-critical-stream connection error.
The control stream's credit comes from the configured limits like every other stream's, rather than being left at whatever the transport defaults to.
A push stream from a client is a typed error of its own rather than an unknown stream.
The push stream header is read before anything is decided, and a stream still waiting for its promise is held on a bounded timer rather than aborted.
A push ID names one push stream: opening a second with the same one is a typed duplicate.
Detecting that duplicate is the typed error the client raises rather than a second stream it accepts.
A reserved stream type decodes to an unknown type and changes nothing about the connection.
Resetting such a stream uses the no-error code.
Each frame type decodes into exactly the fields its description names, and a payload that does not is a typed error rather than a partly read frame.
Bytes left over after a frame's fields, and a payload that ends before them, are both the frame-error connection code.
A frame carrying an inner length has it checked against the frame length rather than trusted, which is what the origin frame's strict framing pins.
A stream ending mid-frame finishes the parser with a typed error rather than with the bytes it had.
Data reaches a message stream or it reaches nothing: the request path routes it through the transaction, and there is no other consumer.
The control stream admits the control frames and unknown types; a data frame on it is the frame-unexpected connection error.

entries.reason: The correction fixes the pseudo-header section's own wording about which fields a CONNECT request omits. The validator already treats CONNECT as its own shape, requiring the authority and refusing the scheme and path, which is what the corrected text says.

The rejected correction would have changed how the field section size is described as being counted. This endpoint advertises its own limit from configuration and bounds what it sends by the peer's advertised one, which is the same behaviour under either wording.

An editorial correction inside a security consideration about padding and traffic analysis. It states nothing this endpoint does differently: no padding decision is taken here, because the transport owns packet construction.

The correction clarifies which stream identifiers a GOAWAY frame may carry in each direction. The control-stream validator already refuses an identifier that is not a client-initiated bidirectional one, which is the corrected reading.
A second proposed correction to the same section, rejected in favour of the one that was verified. This endpoint follows the verified text.

The report concerns how the SETTINGS section describes an endpoint's obligation when it receives an identifier it does not understand. This endpoint preserves such an identifier and reads it with nothing, which satisfies the published text and the reported reading alike.

This package passes one fixed application info and builds the internal value from it exactly as the section specifies, so the clarified reading is the one implemented.

Every status in the inclusive 200 through 299 range is accepted as Extended CONNECT success.

A non-2xx or incomplete Extended CONNECT response returns failure and never unlocks datagram payload.
The stable UDP surface has only the implicitly allocated Context ID zero and exposes no reallocation operation.
An unknown Context ID must be silently dropped or retained only in a short finite registration buffer.
Context ID zero encoding rejects every UDP Proxying Payload longer than 65527 bytes.
Receiving an oversized Context ID zero payload must abort its corresponding request stream.
An oversized UDP datagram carried in a DATAGRAM Capsule should be discarded without buffering its contents.
A datagram arriving before its corresponding request must be silently dropped or buffered for only about one round trip.
Any unknown-context or pre-request datagram buffer should have explicit count and aggregate byte ceilings.
requirements.reason: The receiver deliberately provides no unknown-context or pre-request buffer: it drops before payload parsing or storage and exposes only saturating payload-free counters.

requirements.summary: Forwarding should avoid making target-facing UDP traffic more bursty than the received sequence.
A UDP proxy should not hold packets merely to create larger send batches.
The HTTP/3 transport always gates sends through its CUBIC congestion window and exposes no MASQUE bypass.
A connection that disables congestion control must not advertise Explicit Congestion Notification support.
requirements.reason: Neither the public HTTP configuration nor the QUIC core has a mode that disables congestion control, so the conditional state cannot be entered.

requirements.summary: A connection with disabled congestion control must mark all of its IP packets Not-ECT.
requirements.reason: Congestion control cannot be disabled anywhere in the supported transport configuration, making this conditional marking mode unreachable.

requirements.summary: CONNECT-UDP should use HTTP/3 where possible to retain QUIC DATAGRAM unreliability and avoid nested recovery.
requirements.reason: The building-block API requires an explicit protocol because peer capability and deployment policy are outside this codec; it supports HTTP/3 but does not silently override the caller's selected mapping.

requirements.summary: A target UDP payload too large for a QUIC DATAGRAM should not be converted to a reliable DATAGRAM Capsule.
The proxy should drop an oversized target payload and send an ICMP Packet Too Big response to the target.
The proxy must ignore ECN bits on IP packets carrying UDP datagrams received from the target.
Every UDP packet sent from the proxy to the requested target must use the Not-ECT codepoint.

requirements.summary: SSL 2 is not reachable: both option builders pin the negotiable set to TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2, and the version actually reached is read back and refused if it is anything else.
SSL 3 is outside the same pinned set, and the readback that follows a handshake accepts only 1.2 or 1.3.

TLS 1.0 is below the pinned floor on both sides and cannot be selected; quic_core's own handshake refuses any legacy version field that is not the fixed TLS 1.2 placeholder and negotiates 1.3 through supported_versions.
TLS 1.1 is below the same floor, by the same mechanism.
TLS 1.2 is in the negotiable set on the TCP paths, so a peer that offers nothing newer still completes a handshake.
TLS 1.3 is supported on every path: it is in the negotiable set on the TCP paths and it is the only version quic_core implements.
TLS 1.3 is preferred over TLS 1.2: it is first in the version list both sides offer, and the live loopback handshake settles on 1.3 with both endpoints reporting it.

TLS 1.2 is offered here, so this document's TLS 1.2 rules bind: the cipher list is pinned to the forward-secret AEAD suites rather than inherited, which is what section 4.1 asks of a 1.2 peer, and the version floor excludes every deprecated version.

quic_core is the transport that integrates the handshake here, and it integrates TLS 1.3 only: the engine has no 1.2 state machine, the key schedule is the 1.3 one, and the cipher suites are the three QUIC defines.
This binds the designer of a new application protocol.
requirements.reason: This binds whoever specifies a new application protocol that employs TLS. This package specifies none: it implements HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3, each of which already says how it uses TLS.

requirements.summary: There is no DTLS here to negotiate a version for.
requirements.reason: Neither package implements DTLS. QUIC secures its datagrams with TLS 1.3 carried in CRYPTO frames rather than with a DTLS record layer, and the TCP paths run TLS over a stream. There is no DTLS version to negotiate here, and no DTLS record layer to configure.

requirements.summary: DTLS 1.2 is not implemented.

requirements.reason: Neither package implements DTLS. QUIC secures its datagrams with TLS 1.3 carried in CRYPTO frames rather than with a DTLS record layer, and the TCP paths run TLS over a stream. There is no DTLS version to negotiate here, and no DTLS record layer to configure.

requirements.summary: There is no DTLS version preference to express.
requirements.reason: Neither package implements DTLS. QUIC secures its datagrams with TLS 1.3 carried in CRYPTO frames rather than with a DTLS record layer, and the TCP paths run TLS over a stream. There is no DTLS version to negotiate here, and no DTLS record layer to configure.

requirements.summary: There is no version-fallback retry: a failed handshake is a typed error the caller sees, not a signal to dial again with a lower floor, and the floor itself is fixed in the option builder rather than computed per attempt.
HTTP's TLS-only method is the https scheme, and it is supported: an https request is dialled over TLS from the first byte, and a redirect that would move it to http is refused rather than followed.
Which scheme a deployment asks for is the administrator's.
requirements.reason: This binds the administrator or the service operator who runs a deployment, not the code that is deployed. This package is a library: each connection is configured by its caller, and it operates no service, no domain, and no fleet of its own.

requirements.summary: HTTP is not a protocol whose only path to TLS is a dynamic upgrade.
requirements.reason: This binds a protocol that reaches TLS by upgrading a cleartext connection. HTTP defines a TLS-only method of its own, the https scheme, which is what this client dials and what this server serves; the clause's premise, that only a dynamic upgrade method exists, does not hold.

requirements.summary: The same premise does not hold, and the obligation this half states falls on the administrator besides.
requirements.reason: This binds a protocol that reaches TLS by upgrading a cleartext connection. HTTP defines a TLS-only method of its own, the https scheme, which is what this client dials and what this server serves; the clause's premise, that only a dynamic upgrade method exists, does not hold.

requirements.summary: Strict-Transport-Security is parsed, bounded, and acted on: a verified policy upgrades a later cleartext request for the same host before it is dialled, an IP literal is never recorded as an HSTS host, and only the first field line is read.
Whether a deployment advertises HSTS, and with what lifetime, is the operator's decision, expressed as a response field the handler sets.

requirements.summary: TLS-level compression is not a feature either stack here has.
requirements.reason: TLS-level compression is not implemented on either path. The platform's ssl application offers no compression method to negotiate, so the TCP paths cannot enable one, and TLS 1.3, which is what quic_core implements, removed record compression from the protocol. There is no setting here that could turn it on.

requirements.summary: A ticket leaves the server as AES-256-GCM ciphertext over a fresh nonce with a fixed associated-data label, so its claims are both hidden and authenticated; a tampered or cross-origin ticket does not open.
The ticket cipher is AES-256-GCM whatever the connection negotiated, so it is never weaker than the suite protecting the session it resumes.

A ticket key is a rotatable ring rather than a constant: rotation installs a new current key atomically and is refused if the new key repeats the one it replaces. How often a deployment rotates is its own schedule; that it can, without dropping the connections mid-flight, is what the server provides.
The ring holds the current key and at most one predecessor, so the second rotation drops the oldest key entirely: there is no growing history a stolen key could be drawn from.
Ticket lifetime is bounded at issue and again at storage: a lifetime above the seven-day ceiling is refused rather than clamped, and a ticket past its lifetime does not open.
No TLS 1.2 server here resumes anything: the server option builder disables session reuse outright, so there is no old session for a stolen 1.2 ticket key to reopen.
A resuming client sends a key share in the same ClientHello as its pre-shared key, so the exchange can be completed with fresh key material rather than from the ticket alone.

psk_dhe_ke is the only pre-shared-key exchange mode offered or accepted, so every resumption completes an ephemeral exchange and carries its own forward secrecy; psk_ke is decodable for the wire but never selected.
Which extensions a TLS 1.2 handshake carries is decided inside the handshake implementation.
requirements.reason: This binds the code that builds a TLS 1.2 handshake. This package contains none: the TLS 1.2 path is the platform's ssl application, configured here with the version floor, the cipher list, peer verification, the server name, and the application protocols, and the handshake messages it exchanges inside those bounds are its own. The handshake this package does implement, in quic_core, is TLS 1.3, where this clause has no counterpart.

requirements.summary: The TLS 1.2 ClientHello is not built here.
requirements.reason: This binds the code that builds a TLS 1.2 handshake. This package contains none: the TLS 1.2 path is the platform's ssl application, configured here with the version floor, the cipher list, peer verification, the server name, and the application protocols, and the handshake messages it exchanges inside those bounds are its own. The handshake this package does implement, in quic_core, is TLS 1.3, where this clause has no counterpart.

requirements.summary: Sending a fatal alert on an unacknowledged extension is the 1.2 handshake's own decision.
requirements.reason: This binds the code that builds a TLS 1.2 handshake. This package contains none: the TLS 1.2 path is the platform's ssl application, configured here with the version floor, the cipher list, peer verification, the server name, and the application protocols, and the handshake messages it exchanges inside those bounds are its own. The handshake this package does implement, in quic_core, is TLS 1.3, where this clause has no counterpart.

requirements.summary: extended_master_secret is a TLS 1.2 handshake extension, negotiated by the 1.2 implementation.
requirements.reason: This binds the code that builds a TLS 1.2 handshake. This package contains none: the TLS 1.2 path is the platform's ssl application, configured here with the version floor, the cipher list, peer verification, the server name, and the application protocols, and the handshake messages it exchanges inside those bounds are its own. The handshake this package does implement, in quic_core, is TLS 1.3, where this clause has no counterpart.

requirements.summary: RFC 9113 section 9.2.3 forbids asking a multiplexed connection for a certificate after the handshake, and nothing here does: post-handshake authentication is never requested on the TCP paths, and client authentication in quic_core happens inside the handshake through a CertificateRequest the server sends with its own flight or not at all.

SNI is sent on every dialled connection and read on every accepted one: the TCP client names the host it asked for, and quic_core's server matches the presented name against its credentials, exact names before wildcards, with the pattern grammar enforced.
A server that recognizes no credential for the presented name continues with its default credential instead of stopping.
requirements.reason: An unrecognized server name selects no alternative credential and the handshake proceeds with the server's default one, which the client then either accepts or refuses on identity grounds. A server holding one credential has no other behaviour available, and aborting would turn every name the operator has not enumerated into a handshake failure rather than a certificate mismatch the client reports precisely. The cross-protocol attack this clause is aimed at is closed on the other axis instead: ALPN is required on every connection here, a mismatch is a handshake failure, and the server's own protocol list is authoritative.

requirements.summary: No unrecognized_name alert is generated, because the handshake is not aborted on an unrecognized name.
requirements.reason: This is the positive half of the same sentence: the alert exists only for the abort this server does not perform. The reasoning and the compensating control are the ones recorded on the SHOULD NOT half of the clause, and the alert would be added with it rather than on its own.

requirements.summary: RFC 6066's own text offers two actions, aborting or continuing, and this server takes the second: it understands the extension, matches it against its credentials, and continues with the default credential when no alternative matches.

A certificate that does not match the name the client dialled ends the connection with a typed error before any application byte is written; the TCP path uses the HTTPS match function over the name it sent, and quic_core verifies the service identity itself.

ALPN is carried on both sides of every path: the TCP client advertises its list and the TCP server its preference order, and quic_core negotiates it in the handshake and reports the selected protocol to the connection.
A client list that shares nothing with the server's ends the handshake with no_application_protocol: quic_core raises the typed error and closes with the transport code RFC 7301's alert maps to.

A server that acknowledges ALPN and names a protocol outside the client's list fails the handshake rather than returning a connection; the separate case where a server acknowledges nothing is reported as an unnegotiated protocol, which is not the case this clause describes.
Every connection this package makes or accepts carries ALPN; there is no path that omits it, so a deployment built on this package has it deployed.
Consistency across the several services that answer for one domain name is a property of a deployment, not of a library.
requirements.reason: This binds the administrator or the service operator who runs a deployment, not the code that is deployed. This package is a library: each connection is configured by its caller, and it operates no service, no domain, and no fleet of its own.

requirements.summary: Handling configuration and credential compromise across a fleet of TLS servers is likewise operational.

requirements.summary: 0-RTT is off unless a server opts into it explicitly, and the only application protocol carried over it here is HTTP/3, whose own document says when early data may be sent and what a server does with it. When it is on, a single-use replay guard and a domain-separated fingerprint cache stand in front of it.

A NULL-encryption suite has no AEAD, so the pinned filter excludes it on both sides; quic_core offers only the three AEAD suites QUIC defines. The cipher list is pinned on both the client and the server option builder rather than inherited from the platform default, and the filter that builds it is stated as a predicate over key exchange and MAC, so it tracks whatever the platform considers current inside the bound rather than freezing a list of names.
RC4 is a stream cipher with a separate MAC, which the AEAD half of the pinned filter excludes; it is not in quic_core's suite list either.
Every suite that survives the pin is AES-128 or stronger, or ChaCha20-Poly1305; the export-grade and other sub-112-bit suites carry no AEAD and are gone with the rest.
The weakest suite left is AES-128, so 128 bits is the floor rather than a bound that some offered suite falls below.
Static RSA key transport is not an ephemeral key exchange, and the pinned filter admits only ephemeral ones, so no TLS_RSA_* suite is offered.
Static finite-field Diffie-Hellman is excluded by the same filter: the only key exchanges left are the TLS 1.3 schedule and ECDHE.
Static elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman was the sharpest edge of the platform default, which carried two such suites ahead of the ephemeral finite-field ones; both are outside the pinned filter now.

Forward secrecy is not merely preferred but exhaustive: every suite offered on every path provides it, so there is no ordering under which a peer could reach one that does not. The server also honours its own order rather than the peer's.
The TLS_DHE_* suites the platform offers by default are excluded by the key-exchange half of the filter, on both sides.
The pinned TLS 1.2 list is exactly the ECDHE AEAD family this section recommends, in both its ECDSA and its RSA authentication forms and in both AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.
There is no CBC suite left to need encrypt_then_mac: the filter keeps only AEAD, which settles the clause by removing its subject rather than by negotiating an extension alongside it.
P-256 is the ECDSA scheme quic_core offers first, and it is the curve the key exchange implements alongside X25519; the larger NIST curves are offered after it rather than instead of it.
ECDSA signatures are produced with the platform's randomized nonce rather than RFC 6979's deterministic one.
requirements.reason: RFC 6979 is not implemented here, and the platform's signing primitive is the randomized one. The exposure this recommendation addresses is narrowed from the other side instead: the signature scheme offered first, and the one the loopback credentials use, is Ed25519, whose nonce is derived from the message and the key by construction and cannot repeat, and the elliptic-curve schemes are offered only after it. A deployment that signs with ECDSA gets the platform's nonce generation, which is what this deviation names.

requirements.summary: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 is offered but is not the first proposal.
requirements.reason: The pinned list keeps the platform's own strength ordering, which puts the AES-256 suites ahead of the AES-128 ones, so the first proposal is stronger than the suite this clause names rather than weaker. The clause's own section says in the next paragraph that a client is free to offer stronger suites and that a server should then prefer them, which is what this ordering asks for; reordering to put an AES-128 suite first would mean proposing the weaker of two acceptable suites ahead of the stronger one.

requirements.summary: The server chooses from its own ordered list rather than from the client's proposal order, and that list has no suite weaker than the one this clause names: everything in it is ECDHE and AEAD, at AES-128 or above.
A client that offers AES-256 gets AES-256: the server's order is authoritative and puts the 256-bit suites first, so the stronger proposal wins whenever the client makes one.
TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, and every other suite without forward secrecy, is not merely deprioritised but absent from the pinned list.
quic_core names its groups in supported_groups on both sides of the handshake, and the TCP paths offer the platform's own group list, which every pinned suite needs in order to be usable at all.
X25519 and P-256 are the two groups quic_core implements, each with its own generation, public-value, and shared-secret path, and each validated against its defining document's vectors.
ec_point_formats is a TLS 1.2 extension built by the 1.2 handshake; TLS 1.3 removed it, so quic_core has none to send.
requirements.reason: This binds the code that builds a TLS 1.2 handshake. This package contains none: the TLS 1.2 path is the platform's ssl application, configured here with the version floor, the cipher list, peer verification, the server name, and the application protocols, and the handshake messages it exchanges inside those bounds are its own. The handshake this package does implement, in quic_core, is TLS 1.3, where this clause has no counterpart.

requirements.summary: The packets protected under one key are counted, and crossing the confidentiality limit for the negotiated suite asks for a key update; the update is then driven through the key phase with the spacing the transport requires before another may follow.

Authentication failures are counted separately from encryptions and do not reset on a key update; reaching the integrity limit is a typed failure that ends the connection rather than something the receiver continues past.
The limit enforced is not 2^24.5 records for both versions but the lower per-suite figures RFC 9001 fixes for QUIC.
requirements.reason: RFC 9001 section 6.6 sets its own AEAD limits for QUIC, and those are what this package counts against: 2^23 protected packets for the AES-GCM suites, well under the figure this clause names, and the much larger ChaCha20-Poly1305 figure that document also fixes. Deviating downward for the AES suites is still a deviation from a clause asking for one shared number, and it is recorded as one. The TLS record paths keep the platform's own accounting, which this package does not override.

requirements.summary: There is no finite-field Diffie-Hellman exchange here for a group size to bound.
requirements.reason: No cipher suite offered on any path here uses finite-field Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The TLS 1.2 list is pinned to the ECDHE AEAD suites and TLS 1.3 removed the finite-field groups from the handshake, so no DH group is negotiated and no DH parameter is generated, accepted, or checked.

requirements.summary: The two curves implemented are X25519 and P-256, at 255 and 256 bits; there is no smaller group to select, and an invalid or small-order X25519 public value is refused rather than used.
The modulus belongs to a certificate the caller supplies.
requirements.reason: This binds whoever issues and installs the credential. A server here is handed a certificate chain and a private key that the caller loaded, and a client is handed trust anchors; neither generates a key pair for an identity or chooses a modulus size.

requirements.summary: SHA-256 is the weakest digest in the signature schemes quic_core offers, and the RSA-PSS and ECDSA schemes at that strength are the ones it names first after Ed25519.
Neither SHA-1 nor MD5 appears in the signature schemes offered or accepted; the list is enumerated rather than open, so an unlisted scheme is refused rather than tried.
quic_core's ClientHello carries signature_algorithms with the SHA-256 schemes in it, and a server signature outside that list is refused.
The Truncated HMAC extension is not implemented on either path.
requirements.reason: RFC 6066's truncated_hmac extension is not implemented here. quic_core's extension table enumerates the extensions it encodes and understands and does not include it, so it is neither sent nor honoured, and the platform's ssl application offers no option that would request it on the TCP paths. The extension also only has meaning for a suite with a separate MAC, and every suite offered here is AEAD.

requirements.summary: The reference identity is always the authority in the URI the caller asked for, never a name learned from DNS. The one place a DNS answer reaches this client is the HTTPS record resolver, and what it may contribute is an alternative port on the same origin host; the target name in such a record becomes neither the dialled name nor the verified one.
How a TLS 1.2 record layer forms its GCM nonce is decided inside that record layer.
requirements.reason: This binds the code that builds a TLS 1.2 handshake. This package contains none: the TLS 1.2 path is the platform's ssl application, configured here with the version floor, the cipher list, peer verification, the server name, and the application protocols, and the handshake messages it exchanges inside those bounds are its own. The handshake this package does implement, in quic_core, is TLS 1.3, where this clause has no counterpart.

requirements.summary: No static finite-field Diffie-Hellman key is used, because no finite-field suite is offered.
requirements.reason: No cipher suite offered on any path here uses finite-field Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The TLS 1.2 list is pinned to the ECDHE AEAD suites and TLS 1.3 removed the finite-field groups from the handshake, so no DH group is negotiated and no DH parameter is generated, accepted, or checked.

requirements.summary: There is no ephemeral finite-field key to reuse across connections either.
requirements.reason: No cipher suite offered on any path here uses finite-field Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The TLS 1.2 list is pinned to the ECDHE AEAD suites and TLS 1.3 removed the finite-field groups from the handshake, so no DH group is negotiated and no DH parameter is generated, accepted, or checked.

requirements.summary: No elliptic-curve key is reused: a key pair is generated inside the handshake it serves and is not carried to another. The two groups are X25519, which this clause names as a safe curve, and P-256, whose received point is validated before the shared secret is taken.
No revocation state is consulted on either path: a certificate that chains to a trust anchor and matches the identity is accepted whether or not it has been revoked.
requirements.reason: Neither TLS path here consults revocation state. The TCP paths run the platform's path validation with revocation checking left at its default, which performs none, and quic_core's own path validation builds a chain to a trust anchor and verifies the service identity without reading a CRL, requesting an OCSP response, or asking for a stapled one: status_request is not among the extensions it sends or understands. The trust anchors are the platform store or the set the caller supplies, and narrowing those is the only lever a deployment has here, which is not a strategy for distrusting a certificate that was valid when it was issued and has since been revoked.

requirements.summary: The server supports none of the practices this clause lists as the current foundation, because it has no revocation path at all.
requirements.reason: Neither TLS path here consults revocation state. The TCP paths run the platform's path validation with revocation checking left at its default, which performs none, and quic_core's own path validation builds a chain to a trust anchor and verifies the service identity without reading a CRL, requesting an OCSP response, or asking for a stapled one: status_request is not among the extensions it sends or understands. The trust anchors are the platform store or the set the caller supplies, and narrowing those is the only lever a deployment has here, which is not a strategy for distrusting a certificate that was valid when it was issued and has since been revoked.

requirements.summary: A configurable Maximum Segment Lifetime uses one minute as its recommended value.

requirements.summary: Every incompatible Version Negotiation packet includes every version in the server's Offered Versions set.
A client searches the server's Version Negotiation list for a locally supported version.
A client aborts the connection attempt when the server list contains no eligible mutually supported version.
After finding a mutual version, the client selects it and creates a new first flight using that negotiated version.
Client connection machinery never emits a Version Negotiation packet.
A server silently ignores every received Version Negotiation packet without changing handshake phase.
Version compatibility is allowed only for a pair explicitly specified as compatible.
A server performing non-identity compatible negotiation selects a client-listed version that it supports and knows to be compatible.
requirements.reason: The server accepts the supported Chosen Version and performs only the identity transformation; it never proactively changes the client's first flight to another version, so the conditional non-identity selection path is absent.

requirements.summary: A server aborts the handshake if a selected compatible first flight cannot be converted.
requirements.reason: The shipped server performs no non-identity first-flight conversion and therefore has no conversion failure state; supported client-selected v1 and v2 flights are parsed directly under their wire version.

requirements.summary: A document declaring compatibility between versions specifies how clients learn the negotiated version.
requirements.reason: This is a requirement on specifications that publish a new compatibility relationship, not on endpoint runtime behavior; the separately inventoried RFC 9369 defines the v1/v2 relationship.

requirements.summary: Specifications for mutually compatible versions use the same mechanism for communicating the negotiated version.
requirements.reason: This recommendation governs authors of compatibility specifications rather than endpoint execution; this package implements only the single published v1/v2 relationship defined by RFC 9369.

requirements.summary: Negotiated-version handshake validations also apply to a first flight converted from another compatible version.
requirements.reason: The server does not perform a non-identity first-flight conversion; each v1 or v2 first flight is authenticated, decoded, and validated directly under the version carried on that connection.

requirements.summary: The default Original Version policy tries to avoid the extra round trip of incompatible negotiation.

A client ignores a Version Negotiation packet that contains its Original Version.

Both endpoints parse peer Version Information as a bounded authenticated transport parameter.
Malformed Version Information causes the endpoint to close the connection rather than continue the handshake.
A QUIC v1 Version Information parse failure closes with TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR code 0x08.
A zero Chosen Version or zero Available Version is treated as a Version Information parsing failure.
A server treats client Version Information as malformed when Chosen Version is absent from Available Versions.
Every supported negotiating QUIC version has a wire-visible VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR close path.
The server validates that the client's authenticated Chosen Version equals the connection's negotiated version.

A client reacting to Version Negotiation does not complete when authenticated server Version Information is missing, except for the v1 legacy rule.
The client closes when the server's authenticated Chosen Version was absent from the client's Available Versions.
Missing authenticated server Version Information after a Version Negotiation exchange produces VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR, subject to the v1 exception.
A client that acted on Version Negotiation validates the authenticated server Available Versions against its preference order.
The client closes if authenticated server support would have caused it to choose a different negotiated version.
After acting on Version Negotiation, the client rejects an empty server Available Versions list.
The client validates that authenticated server Chosen Version equals the negotiated connection version.
A server Chosen Version mismatch closes the client connection with VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR code 0x11.
Server operators use the specified three-step Offered, Acceptable, and Fully Deployed version rollout sequence.
requirements.reason: This library exposes one immutable supported-version set and no fleet deployment mutation API, so it cannot perform an operator rollout; the centralized policy explicitly records the required MSL-gated design if mutation is added.

requirements.reason: This requirement applies to authors designing a future QUIC version, while this package implements published v1 and v2 and does not define a new version specification.

requirements.summary: TLS session tickets are tightly bound to one QUIC version and are rejected across versions by both endpoints.

requirements.summary: Both endpoints derive and send Handshake and 1-RTT protection under the negotiated QUIC version.

The client never applies a v1 TLS ticket or paired NEW_TOKEN to a v2 initial connection, or v2 resumption state to a v1 initial connection.

requirements.summary: A TCP sender cannot send sequence data beyond the minimum of its congestion and receiver windows.
requirements.reason: This package implements QUIC rather than TCP: QUIC has no TCP sequence-number or rwnd state, and its independent congestion and stream/connection flow-control gates are mapped under RFC 9002 and RFC 9000.

requirements.summary: HyStart++ uses the recommended RTT thresholds, sample count, CSS divisor, CSS rounds, and paced growth limit.

The paced controller applies all newly acknowledged bytes without the non-paced eight-datagram cap.
HyStart++ runs only for the initial slow start and is disabled after congestion or completed CSS.

requirements.summary: A profile is an explicit value naming the components that must be covered, the maximum age a signature may have, the tolerated clock skew, whether a nonce is required, and the authority and tag it binds to; none of them has a default and an empty one is refused.

requirements.summary: Every step of base generation returns a typed error that ends it: no partial base is returned and nothing is signed from one.

Signing is the stated sequence and nothing else: build the base, check the algorithm against the key, compute the MAC, and emit both fields together.
Key material is validated when it is constructed and is of one kind, so the key handed to the signer is always one the algorithm can use.

Verification is the stated sequence: parse both fields, pair them by label, check the time bounds and the profile, rebuild the base, compare the MAC in constant time, and only then consume the nonce.
